mcq.q: Anil, Babu and Chetan jointly promise to pay Dev ₹90,000. Dev recovers the full ₹90,000 from Anil alone. Which is correct?
options: Dev must sue all three together
Dev may do so; Anil can claim contribution of ₹30,000 each from Babu and Chetan — Section 43
Dev may recover only ₹30,000 from Anil
Anil cannot claim any contribution
mcq.explain: Section 43 lets the promisee, unless they agreed otherwise, demand the whole performance from any single joint promisor, or from several of them. A joint promisor who pays more than his share may compel the others to contribute equally — ₹90,000 ÷ 3 = ₹30,000 each.
mcq.fast: Joint promisors: creditor can catch any one for the whole; payer then recovers equal shares.

mcq.q: Of three joint promisors, one becomes insolvent and cannot contribute. Under Section 43, the loss arising from his default is borne by:
options: The promisee
The remaining joint promisors in equal shares
The insolvent promisor's legal heirs only
The joint promisor who paid first, alone
mcq.explain: Under Section 43, when one co-promisor fails to pay his share, the loss caused by his failure is split equally among the others. The promisee still gets full performance; the solvent co-promisors share the burden equally among themselves.
mcq.fast: Default of one co-promisor -> the others share it EQUALLY.

mcq.q: A contract fixes no time for performance, and the promisor need not wait for a demand. Under Section 46, he must perform:
options: Immediately on the same day
Within 30 days
Within a reasonable time
Whenever he likes
mcq.explain: Section 46: where no date is fixed and no demand is needed, the promise is to be carried out within a reasonable time. What is reasonable is a question of fact in each case. No fixed number of days is laid down by the Act.
mcq.fast: No time fixed = reasonable time. The Act never fixes "30 days" here.

mcq.q: A debtor owes a creditor several debts and pays a sum without saying which debt it is for; the creditor also makes no appropriation. Under Section 61, the payment is applied to:
options: The largest debt first
The debts in order of time (oldest first)
The debt carrying the highest interest first
All debts proportionately in every case
mcq.explain: Section 59 lets the debtor appropriate; failing him, Section 60 lets the creditor choose. If neither makes a choice, Section 61 sets the money against the debts chronologically, oldest first, even time-barred ones. Only if the debts are of equal standing is it applied proportionately.
mcq.fast: Debtor first (s.59) -> creditor (s.60) -> law: chronological order (s.61).

mcq.q: Old contract out, fresh contract in (same or different parties) — this is called:
options: Novation — Section 62
Remission — Section 63
Rescission by breach
Alteration under Section 39
mcq.explain: Under Section 62, the original contract need not be performed if the parties agree to replace, cancel or alter it. Replacement by a fresh contract is called novation. Remission under Section 63 is accepting less than was promised; Section 39 deals with refusal to perform.
mcq.topic: Contracts that need not be performed (Sections 62–67)
mcq.fast: NEW contract replaces old = Novation. Accept LESS = Remission.

mcq.q: Under Section 63, a creditor owed ₹1,00,000 agrees in writing to accept ₹70,000 in full settlement and receives it. The creditor:
options: Can claim ₹30,000 because no consideration was given for remission
Can claim ₹30,000 with interest
Can rescind and claim ₹1,00,000
Cannot later claim the balance of ₹30,000
mcq.explain: Section 63 allows a promisee to waive all or part of what was promised, to give more time, or to accept any satisfaction he chooses. Indian law does not require fresh consideration for remission, so acceptance of ₹70,000 in full satisfaction discharges the whole debt.
mcq.topic: Contracts that need not be performed (Sections 62–67)
mcq.fast: Section 63: promisee may accept less — no new consideration needed.

mcq.q: Supervening impossibility, which makes a contract void when the act becomes impossible after the contract is made, is dealt with in:
options: Section 73
Section 56
Section 25
Section 70
mcq.explain: Section 56 covers two cases: an agreement to do something impossible is void from the start, and a contract whose performance later turns impossible or unlawful becomes void at that point. This is the Indian doctrine of frustration. Section 73 is damages, Section 25 is consideration and Section 70 is quasi contract.
mcq.topic: Contracts that need not be performed (Sections 62–67)

mcq.q: Which event does NOT discharge a contract by supervening impossibility?
options: Destruction of the specific subject matter without fault of either party
Death of a singer engaged personally for a concert
Outbreak of war making performance unlawful
The cost of performance rises sharply because raw material prices doubled
mcq.explain: Frustration under Section 56 needs the act itself to become impossible or unlawful. Destruction of the subject matter, death or incapacity in personal contracts, and change of law or war all qualify. Mere commercial hardship, higher cost or lower profit does not frustrate a contract; the promisor must still perform.
mcq.topic: Contracts that need not be performed (Sections 62–67)

mcq.q: A contract to paint a portrait is made with a famous artist. Who must perform it?
options: The artist personally, as the contract depends on personal skill — Section 40
Any competent painter the artist appoints
The artist's legal heirs after his death
Any person the promisee chooses
mcq.explain: Under Section 40, where the parties clearly meant the promisor to do the work himself, nobody else can do it for him. A contract relying on the personal skill of an artist cannot be performed by an agent or by legal representatives.
mcq.topic: By whom must a contract be performed? (Sections 40–42)
mcq.fast: Personal skill or confidence -> only the promisor himself.
